messages.subject: Extension of the JS Model as a multistate model with multiple states
messages.subject_clean: Extension of the JS Model as a multistate model with multiple states
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

Foreword: This is my first post, so please forgive me if my question is inappropriate for this list, let me know and I will adjust.

I have adapted the code in chapter 10 of the Kéry and Schaub book that fits the JS model as a multistate model but instead of having just 3 states: not yet entered, alive and dead, I have 3 additional alive states so in total 5: not yet entered, breeders, non-breeder, juveniles and dead. I have changed the state transition matrix and the observation matrix accordingly. The main change is that instead of having only one entry probability (gamma), I have one entry probability per alive state. My code runs properly on a simplified subset of my data. However I would like to be sure that I am correctly implementing the changes to the prior and the calculation of the population parameters. If someone could have a look at my model below, I would be very grateful. I have not shared a dataset, however, if you want one to play around with the model, I can provide one.

Many thanks!

Tina

 model {

    #--------------------------------------
    # Parameters:
    # phi: survival probability
    # gamma: removal entry probability
    # p: capture probability
    #--------------------------------------
    # States (S):
    # 1 not yet entered
    # 2 Breeder
    # 3 Non breeder
    # 4 Juvenile
    # 5 dead
    # Observations (O):
    # 1 seen as breeder
    # 2 seen as non-breeder
    # 3 seen as juvenile
    # 4 not seen
    #--------------------------------------

    # Priors and constraints
    for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){

    phiB[t] <- mean.phi.1
    phiNB[t]<- mean.phi.2
    phiJ[t] <- mean.phi.3

    psiBNB[t] <- mean.psi.1
    psiNBB[t]<- mean.psi.2

    pB[t] <- mean.p.1
    pNB[t] <- mean.p.2
    pJ[t]<- mean.p.3

    #dirichlet dist to make sure that all the gammas (+1) sum to one.
for (k in 1:4){
beta[k, t] ~ dgamma(1, 1)
gamma[k, t]<-beta[k,t]/sum(beta[,t])

}

    }

    mean.phi.1 ~ dunif(0, 1)
    mean.phi.2 ~ dunif(0, 1)
    mean.phi.3 ~ dunif(0, 1)

    mean.psi.1 ~ dunif(0, 1)
    mean.psi.2 ~ dunif(0, 1)

    mean.p.1 ~ dunif(0, 1)
    mean.p.2 ~ dunif(0, 1)
    mean.p.3 ~ dunif(0, 1)

    # Define state-transition and observation matrices
    for (i in 1:M){
    # Define probabilities of state S(t+1) given S(t)
    for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
    ps[1,i,t,1]<- 1 - (gamma[1,t] + gamma[2,t] + gamma[3,t])
    ps[1,i,t,2]<- gamma[1,t]
    ps[1,i,t,3]<- gamma[2,t]
    ps[1,i,t,4]<- gamma[3,t]
    ps[1,i,t,5]<- 0

    ps[2,i,t,1] <- 0
    ps[2,i,t,2] <- phiB[t] * (1-psiBNB[t])
    ps[2,i,t,3] <- phiB[t] * psiBNB[t]
    ps[2,i,t,4] <- 0
    ps[2,i,t,5] <- 1-phiB[t]

    ps[3,i,t,1] <- 0
    ps[3,i,t,2] <- phiNB[t] * psiNBB[t]
    ps[3,i,t,3] <- phiNB[t] * (1-psiNBB[t])
    ps[3,i,t,4] <- 0
    ps[3,i,t,5] <- 1-phiNB[t]

    ps[4,i,t,1] <- 0
    ps[4,i,t,2] <- 0
    ps[4,i,t,3] <- phiJ[t]
    ps[4,i,t,4] <- 0
    ps[4,i,t,5] <- 1- phiJ[t]

    ps[5,i,t,1] <- 0
    ps[5,i,t,2] <- 0
    ps[5,i,t,3] <- 0
    ps[5,i,t,4] <- 0
    ps[5,i,t,5] <- 1

    # Define probabilities of O(t) given S(t)
    po[1,i,t,1] <- 0
    po[1,i,t,2] <- 0
    po[1,i,t,3] <- 0
    po[1,i,t,4] <- 1

    po[2,i,t,1] <- pB[t]
    po[2,i,t,2] <- 0
    po[2,i,t,3] <- 0
    po[2,i,t,4] <- 1-pB[t]

    po[3,i,t,1] <- pNB[t]
    po[3,i,t,2] <- 0
    po[3,i,t,3] <- 0
    po[3,i,t,4] <- 1-pNB[t]

    po[4,i,t,1] <- pJ[t]
    po[4,i,t,2] <- 0
    po[4,i,t,3] <- 0
    po[4,i,t,4] <- 1-pJ[t]

    po[5,i,t,1] <- 0
    po[5,i,t,2] <- 0
    po[5,i,t,3] <- 0
    po[5,i,t,4] <- 1
    } #t
    } #i

    # Likelihood
    for (i in 1:M){
    # Define latent state at first occasion
    z[i,1] <- 1   # Make sure that all M individuals are in state 1 at t=1
    for (t in 2:n.occasions){
    # State process: draw S(t) given S(t-1)
    z[i,t] ~ dcat(ps[z[i,t-1], i, t-1,])

    # Observation process: draw O(t) given S(t)
    y[i,t] ~ dcat(po[z[i,t], i, t-1,])
    } #t
    } #i

    # Calculate derived population parameters
    for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
    qgamma[t] <- 1-gamma[1,t]-gamma[2,t]-gamma[3,t]
    }
    cprob[1] <- gamma[1,1]+gamma[2,1]+gamma[3,1]
    for (t in 2:(n.occasions-1)){
    cprob[t] <- (gamma[1,t]-gamma[2,t]-gamma[3,t]) * prod(qgamma[1:(t-1)])
    } #t
    psi <- sum(cprob[])            # Inclusion probability
    for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
    b[t] <- cprob[t] / psi      # Entry probability
    } #t

    for (i in 1:M){
    for (t in 2:n.occasions){
    Bal[i,t-1] <- equals(z[i,t], 2)
    NBal[i,t-1] <- equals(z[i,t], 3)
    Jal[i,t-1] <- equals(z[i,t], 4)
    } #t
    for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
    d[i,t] <- equals(z[i,t]-Bal[i,t]- NBal[i,t]-Jal[i,t],0)
    } #t
    Balive[i] <- sum(Bal[i,])
    NBalive[i] <- sum(NBal[i,])
    Jalive[i] <- sum(Jal[i,])
    alive[i]<- sum(Bal[i,])+sum(NBal[i,])+sum(Jal[i,])
    } #i

    for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
    N[t] <- sum(Bal[,t])+sum(NBal[,t])+sum(Jal[,t])     # Actual population size
    B[t] <- sum(d[,t])         # Number of entries
    } #t
    for (i in 1:M){
    w[i] <- 1-equals(alive[i],0)
    } #i
    Nsuper <- sum(w[])            # Superpopulation size
    }

messages.body_plain:
Eric,

So you failed to collect snails at all during the capture or recapture sessions in ponds 1 and 7?  If you want to include these ponds, a zero-inflated distribution might provide better fit if p is constant.  My guess is that the expected value of N is sufficiently large that the probability of having population = 0 snails in any pond is almost impossible under Poisson or NB distributions (hence the expected values are uniformly larger than the observed?).  Also, I would not fit a model with a factorial, site-specific p: again, there's no information in the data to allow estimation of the parameter for those ponds with no encounters.  Maybe a treatment-specific p would work.

Actually, scratch that last sentence: I think an additional problem is that the replication is 3 at each treatment level, and it is almost impossible to find an appropriate distribution for lambda or p given that level of replication.  For example, treatment 1 (if I'm reading this correctly) has one pond with no detections whatsoever ,1 pond where 1 snail was encountered twice, and one pond where 30 animals were observed 11, and 12 animals 01.  So in one pond, the expected value of p (if these were treated independently) is 0, in the next it is 1, and in the final it is...uh, I dunno, 0.8 or something?  That's a tough to fit to a distribution.  Similarly, the expected values of N at those sites would be ~infinity, 1, and 50 or something.  Tough to find a good parametric fit there, either.    Yeah, in general, it looks like p is extremely high, but you have a couple of sites with very few--if any--snails.  I think a ZIP or ZINB is the way to go, and maybe the zero inflation parameter is best modeled as a function of treatment as well.

John

> 1) I don't really know how to deal with the two ponds (#1 and #7) in which no snail was observed (i.e., all intially introduced snails died, which is obviously a strong indication of an experimental effect). For now I use one single 00 capture history for each of these snail-absent ponds. Increasing number of 00 observations (to 20 and 100, obs object in the code) does not affect estimates of total N (the sum of all population sizes) or capture probability p, but strongly homogenizes group membership probabilities (such that estimated pop sizes become quite similar among ponds). Also, DIC increases.

> 2) I have a complete lack of fit (bayesian p-value of 0, very large ratio of Eobs and Esim). I have tried the negative binomial version of the model in Royle, Converse and Link 2012 (see second code pasted below) but get all negative estimates. messages.subject: Hierarchical Lincoln-Petersen model: epilogue
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

after all here is a fitting model for my problem (hopefully this code will be useful to someone). I used an overdispersed poisson distribution. As John pointed out, given the very large variability and low number of replicates I was unlikely to find any significant effect of the treatments on snail population size. And this is indeed the case. However, I have learnt a lot and am more than ever happy with using JAGS and hierarchical models. Thank you all for your help!

éric

cat(file = "Lincoln_petersen_poisson.jags", "
model{
##### PRIORS AND CONSTRAINTS
# abundance model
  for(i in 1:M){
        g[i] ~ dcat(gprobs[])
        z[i] ~ dbern(psi)
    }
  psi <- sum(lam[])/M
  for(j in 1:tr){
    beta[j] ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
    }
  tau.lam <- pow(sd.lam, -2)
  sd.lam ~ dunif(0, 10)
# detection model
  for(i in 1:M){
        treat.long[i] ~ dcat(tprobs[])
    }
for(j in 1:tr){
    gamma[j] ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
    tprobs[j] ~ dunif(0,1)
        }
##### LIKELIHOOD
# abundance model
  for(s in 1:S){
    gprobs[s] <- lam[s]/sum(lam[])
        log(lam[s]) <- beta[treat[s]] + eps[s]
        eps[s] ~ dnorm(0, tau.lam)
    }
# detection model
  for(i in 1:M){
        y[i] ~ dbin(mu[i], K)
       mu[i] <- z[i]*p[i]
    p[i] <- exp(lp[i])/(1+exp(lp[i]))
       lp[i] <- gamma[treat.long[i]]
    }
##### GOODNESS OF FIT
  for(s in 1:S){
        Eobs[s] <- pow(tobs[s] - sum(tobs[])*gprobs[s], 2) / (sum(tobs[])*gprobs[s])
        Esim[s] <- pow(lam[s]*cprob[s] - sum(lam[])*gprobs[s], 2) / (sum(lam[])*gprobs[s])
  }

#### DERIVED QUANTITIES
cprob[1] <-  1/(1+exp(-gamma[1]))
cprob[5] <-  1/(1+exp(-gamma[1]))
cprob[9] <-  1/(1+exp(-gamma[1]))
cprob[2] <-  1/(1+exp(-gamma[2]))
cprob[6] <-  1/(1+exp(-gamma[2]))
cprob[10] <- 1/(1+exp(-gamma[2]))
cprob[3] <-  1/(1+exp(-gamma[3]))
cprob[7] <-  1/(1+exp(-gamma[3]))
cprob[11] <- 1/(1+exp(-gamma[3]))
cprob[4] <-  1/(1+exp(-gamma[4]))
cprob[8] <-  1/(1+exp(-gamma[4]))
cprob[12] <- 1/(1+exp(-gamma[4]))
fit <- sum(Eobs[])
fit.new <http://fit.new> <- sum(Esim[])
}
")

messages.subject: How to fix some parameters in multi-state models with fixed group effects
messages.subject_clean: How to fix some parameters in multi-state models with fixed group effects
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am currently working on a multi-state known fate model to investigate cause-specific mortality (hunting and other sources of mortality).
I was able to write and to run such a model in my situation with 3 differents sites (no dispersion) and with 2 groups (wild or released individuals).
I reduced the time effect to a seasonal effect using a covariate for each occasion.
The model is able to estimate quite well all parameters. However, there is no hunting for 2 sites, and the hunting mortality is estimated in the range: 0.00-0.10, not clearly 0 ...
Therefore, I would like to fix the hunting mortality to 0 for these 2 sites to avoid some bias in the estimation.

I tried to define separately the a[,,,] fixed to 0 and those that will be estimated but it doesn't work.

If you have some tricks, they are welcome !

Thanks for the help.
Best wishes,

Guillaume

here is the current working code:

# Import dataset
data <- read.table("PR_real.txt",header=F,sep="\t")
colnames(data) <- c(seq(1,92,1),"sexe","Mage","Origin","site")
n.ind <- dim(data)[1]
## creater vectors to collect information on origin, site, sex
origin <- c(rep(NA,n.ind))
site <- as.numeric(data[,"site"])
sex <- as.numeric(data[,"sexe"])
for (i in 1:n.ind){
  or <- as.numeric(data[,"Origin"]) # 2 levels: R & W => R=1 & W=2
  if (or[i]==1){ # if bird is a released bird
    origin[i] <- 2
  } else {
    origin[i] <- 1
  }
}
origin
site
sex

## create matrix with capture histories only
CH <- matrix(as.matrix(data[,1:92]),ncol=ncol(data[,1:92]),dimnames=NULL)
head(CH)

## create vector to categorize the season
# marking began in April, thus first month in study = April
# year = 5 months of "Breeding", 3 months of "Hunting" and 4 months of "Other"
n.years <- dim(CH)[2]%/%12 # number of complete years on the data set
left <- dim(CH)[2]%%12  # number of left months
season <- c(rep(c(rep(1,5),rep(2,3),rep(3,4)),n.years),c(rep(1,5),rep(2,3)))

# Create vector with occasion of marking
get.first <- function(x) min(which(x!=0))
f <- apply(CH, 1, get.first)

# Recode CH matrix: note, a 0 is not allowed!
# 1 = alive, 2 = recovered Hunted, 3 = recovered Dead, 4 = not detected
rMR <- CH  # Recoded CH
rMR[rMR==0] <- 4

# Specify model in BUGS language
sink("msmr.bug")
cat("
    model {

    # -------------------------------------------------
    # Parameters:
    # mH=m[1]         Hunting mortality probability
    # mN=m[2]         Natural mortality probability
    # m[3]=1-sum(m[]) survival prob
    # l:              loss of signal from radiotracking device
    # -------------------------------------------------
    # States (S):
    # 1 alive and active transmitter
    # 2 alive but inactive transmitter (not observable)
    # 3 recently dead and recovered hunted
    # 4 recently dead and recovered
    # 5 Dead (absorbing, not observable)
    # Observations (O):
    # 1 detected alive
    # 2 recovered Hunted
    # 3 recovered dead
    # 4 not detected
    # -------------------------------------------------

    ## Priors and constraints
    # Prior for loss of signal
    for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
      l[t]  <- l.seas[season[t]]
    }
    for (s in 1:3){
      l.seas[s] ~ dunif(0,1)
    }

    # fixed time and groups effect for survival and cause-specific mortality
    for (i in 1:nind){ #ind
      for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){ #time -> season
        for (b in 1:3){ # which parameters 1=mH,2=mN,3=S
          m[b,t,i,i] <- m.comp[b,season[t],site[i],origin[i]]
        }
      }
    }
    # dirichlet prior for mortality and survival
    for (b in 1:3){ #param              1=mH,2=mN,3=S
      for (t in 1:3){ #season           1=Breed,2=Hunt,3=Other
        for (s in 1:3){ #site              1=Lu,2=Pa,3=Po
          for (k in 1:2){ #origin         1=W,2=R
            a[b,t,s,k] ~ dgamma(1,1)
            m.comp[b,t,s,k] <- a[b,t,s,k]/sum(a[,t,s,k])    # m.comp[1,t,1,1] & m.comp[1,t,3,1] should be fixed to 0
          }
        }
      }
    }

   }

    for (b in 2:3){ #param              1=mH,2=mN,3=S

      for (t in 1:3){ #season           1=Breed,2=Hunt,3=Other

        for (s in 1:3){ #site              1=Lu,2=Pa,3=Po

          for (k in 1:2){ #origin         1=W,2=R

            a[b,t,s,k] ~ dgamma(1,1)

Betreff: How to fix some parameters in multi-state models with fixed group effects

Dear all,

I am currently working on a multi-state known fate model to investigate cause-specific mortality (hunting and other sources of mortality).

I was able to write and to run such a model in my situation with 3 differents sites (no dispersion) and with 2 groups (wild or released individuals).

I reduced the time effect to a seasonal effect using a covariate for each occasion.

The model is able to estimate quite well all parameters. However, there is no hunting for 2 sites, and the hunting mortality is estimated in the range: 0.00-0.10, not clearly 0 ...

Therefore, I would like to fix the hunting mortality to 0 for these 2 sites to avoid some bias in the estimation.

I tried to define separately the a[,,,] fixed to 0 and those that will be estimated but it doesn't work.

If you have some tricks, they are welcome !

Thanks for the help.

Best wishes,

Guillaume

messages.body_plain:
Dear Michi,

Thanks for the tips.
After several trials to fix m.comp outside the loop, it finally worked for my study case (no hunting mortality [mH] for wild birds in 2 sites, no released birds on those 2 sites, no mH for 2 seasons on the 3rd site for both wild and released birds).
Now only real parameters are estimated.

Thanks.

Best regards,
Guillaume

Here is the final code:

model {

    # -------------------------------------------------
    # Parameters:
    # mH=m[1]         Hunting mortality probability
    # mN=m[2]         Natural mortality probability
    # m[3]=1-sum(m[]) survival prob
    # l:              loss of signal from radiotracking device
    # -------------------------------------------------
    # States (S):
    # 1 alive and active transmitter
    # 2 alive but inactive transmitter (not observable)
    # 3 recently dead and recovered hunted
    # 4 recently dead and recovered
    # 5 Dead (absorbing, not observable)
    # Observations (O):
    # 1 detected alive
    # 2 recovered Hunted
    # 3 recovered dead
    # 4 not detected
    # -------------------------------------------------

    ## Priors and constraints
    # Prior for loss of signal
    for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
      l[t]  <- l.seas[season[t]]
    }
    for (s in 1:3){
      l.seas[s] ~ dunif(0,1)
    }

    ## overall dirichlet prior for mortality and survival

    for (i in 1:nind){ #ind
      for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){ #time -> season
        for (b in 1:3){ # which parameters

          m[b,t,i,i] <- m.comp[b,season[t],site[i],origin[i]]
        }
      }
    }

    ## Individuals in Luberon and Porquerolles
    # fixing values for wild ind

    for (t in 1:3){

      for (s in 2:3){
        m.comp[1,t,s,1] <- 0
      }
    }
    # fixing values for released ind

    for (t in 1:3){

      for (b in 1:3){

        for (s in 2:3){
          m.comp[b,t,s,2] <- 0
        }
      }
    }

    # priors for parameters to be estimated

    for (b in 2:3){ #param

      for (t in 1:3){ #season

        for (s in 2:3){ #site only Lu(2) and Po(3)
          a[b,t,s,1] ~ dgamma(1,1)
          m.comp[b,t,s,1] <- a[b,t,s,1]/sum(a[2:3,t,s,1])
        }
      }
    }

    ## Individuals in Pailhès
    # fixing hunting mortality for both wild and released birds
    for (t in 2:3){

      for (k in 1:2){

        m.comp[1,t,1,k] <- 0
      }
    }
    # priors for parameters (mH,mN,S) for hunting season in Pailhès

    for (b in 1:3){ #param

      for (k in 1:2){ #origin

        a[b,1,1,k] ~ dgamma(1,1)
        m.comp[b,1,1,k] <- a[b,1,1,k]/sum(a[,1,1,k])
      }
    }

    # priors for parameters for other seasons in Pailhès

    for (b in 2:3){ #param

      for (t in 2:3){ #season

        for (k in 1:2){ #origin

          a[b,t,1,k] ~ dgamma(1,1)
          m.comp[b,t,1,k] <- a[b,t,1,k]/sum(a[2:3,t,1,k])

        }
      }
    }

    ## Define state-transition and observation matrices
    for (i in 1:nind){
      # Define probabilities of state S(t+1) given S(t)
      for (t in f[i]:(n.occasions-1)){
        ps[1,i,t,1] <- (1-l[t])*m[3,t,i,i]
        ps[1,i,t,2] <- l[t]
        ps[1,i,t,3] <- (1-l[t])*m[1,t,i,i]
        ps[1,i,t,4] <- (1-l[t])*m[2,t,i,i]
        ps[1,i,t,5] <- 0
        ps[2,i,t,1] <- 0
        ps[2,i,t,2] <- 1
        ps[2,i,t,3] <- 0
        ps[2,i,t,4] <- 0
        ps[2,i,t,5] <- 0
        ps[3,i,t,1] <- 0
        ps[3,i,t,2] <- 0
        ps[3,i,t,3] <- 0
        ps[3,i,t,4] <- 0
        ps[3,i,t,5] <- 1
        ps[4,i,t,1] <- 0
        ps[4,i,t,2] <- 0
        ps[4,i,t,3] <- 0
        ps[4,i,t,4] <- 0
        ps[4,i,t,5] <- 1
        ps[5,i,t,1] <- 0
        ps[5,i,t,2] <- 0
        ps[5,i,t,3] <- 0
        ps[5,i,t,4] <- 0
        ps[5,i,t,5] <- 1

        # Define probabilities of O(t) given S(t)
        po[1,i,t,1] <- 1
        po[1,i,t,2] <- 0
        po[1,i,t,3] <- 0
        po[1,i,t,4] <- 0
        po[2,i,t,1] <- 0
        po[2,i,t,2] <- 0
        po[2,i,t,3] <- 0
        po[2,i,t,4] <- 1
        po[3,i,t,1] <- 0
        po[3,i,t,2] <- 1
        po[3,i,t,3] <- 0
        po[3,i,t,4] <- 0
        po[4,i,t,1] <- 0
        po[4,i,t,2] <- 0
        po[4,i,t,3] <- 1
        po[4,i,t,4] <- 0
        po[5,i,t,1] <- 0
        po[5,i,t,2] <- 0
        po[5,i,t,3] <- 0
        po[5,i,t,4] <- 1
      } #t
    } #i

    # Likelihood
    for (i in 1:nind){
      # Define latent state at first capture   # all individuals are captured as alive and active radiotracker => 1
      z[i,f[i]] <- 1
      for (t in (f[i]+1):n.occasions){
        # State process: draw S(t) given S(t-1)
        z[i,t] ~ dcat(ps[z[i,t-1], i, t-1,])
        # Observation process: draw O(t) given S(t)
        y[i,t] ~ dcat(po[z[i,t], i, t-1,])
      } #t
    } #i
  }
",fill = TRUE)
sink()

> get.first <- function(x) min(which(x!=0))
>
> f <- apply(CH, 1, get.first)
>
>
>
> # Recode CH matrix: note, a 0 is not allowed!
>
> # 1 = alive, 2 = recovered Hunted, 3 = recovered Dead, 4 = not detected
>
> rMR <- CH  # Recoded CH
>
> rMR[rMR==0] <- 4
>
>
>
> # Specify model in BUGS language
>
> sink("msmr.bug")
>
> cat("
>
>     model {
>
>
>
>     # -------------------------------------------------
>
>     # Parameters:
>
>     # mH=m[1]         Hunting mortality probability
>
>     # mN=m[2]         Natural mortality probability
>
>     # m[3]=1-sum(m[]) survival prob
>
>     # l:              loss of signal from radiotracking device
>
>     # -------------------------------------------------
>
>     # States (S):
>
>     # 1 alive and active transmitter
>
>     # 2 alive but inactive transmitter (not observable)
>
>     # 3 recently dead and recovered hunted
>
>     # 4 recently dead and recovered
>
>     # 5 Dead (absorbing, not observable)
>
>     # Observations (O):
>
>     # 1 detected alive
>
>     # 2 recovered Hunted
>
>     # 3 recovered dead
>
>     # 4 not detected
>
>     # -------------------------------------------------
>
>
>
>     ## Priors and constraints
>
>     # Prior for loss of signal
>
>     for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
>
>       l[t]  <- l.seas[season[t]]
>
>     }
>
>     for (s in 1:3){
>
>       l.seas[s] ~ dunif(0,1)
>
>     }
>
>
>
>     # fixed time and groups effect for survival and cause-specific mortality
>
>     for (i in 1:nind){ #ind
>
>       for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){ #time -> season
>
>         for (b in 1:3){ # which parameters 1=mH,2=mN,3=S
>
>           m[b,t,i,i] <- m.comp[b,season[t],site[i],origin[i]]
>
>         }
>
>       }
>
>     }
>
>     # dirichlet prior for mortality and survival
>
>     for (b in 1:3){ #param              1=mH,2=mN,3=S
>
>       for (t in 1:3){ #season           1=Breed,2=Hunt,3=Other
>
>         for (s in 1:3){ #site              1=Lu,2=Pa,3=Po
>
>           for (k in 1:2){ #origin         1=W,2=R
>
>             a[b,t,s,k] ~ dgamma(1,1)
>
>             m.comp[b,t,s,k] <- a[b,t,s,k]/sum(a[,t,s,k])    # m.comp[1,t,1,1] & m.comp[1,t,3,1] should be fixed to 0
>
>           }
>
>         }
>
>       }
>
>     }
>
>
>
>     ## Define state-transition and observation matrices
>
>     for (i in 1:nind){
>
>     # Define probabilities of state S(t+1) given S(t)
>
>     for (t in f[i]:(n.occasions-1)){
>
>     ps[1,i,t,1] <- (1-l[t])*m[3,t,i,i]
>
>     ps[1,i,t,2] <- l[t]
>
>     ps[1,i,t,3] <- (1-l[t])*m[1,t,i,i]
>
>     ps[1,i,t,4] <- (1-l[t])*m[2,t,i,i]
>
>     ps[1,i,t,5] <- 0
>
>     ps[2,i,t,1] <- 0
>
>     ps[2,i,t,2] <- 1
>
>     ps[2,i,t,3] <- 0
>
>     ps[2,i,t,4] <- 0
>
>     ps[2,i,t,5] <- 0
>
>     ps[3,i,t,1] <- 0
>
>     ps[3,i,t,2] <- 0
>
>     ps[3,i,t,3] <- 0
>
>     ps[3,i,t,4] <- 0
>
>     ps[3,i,t,5] <- 1
>
>     ps[4,i,t,1] <- 0
>
>     ps[4,i,t,2] <- 0
>
>     ps[4,i,t,3] <- 0
>
>     ps[4,i,t,4] <- 0
>
>     ps[4,i,t,5] <- 1
>
>     ps[5,i,t,1] <- 0
>
>     ps[5,i,t,2] <- 0
>
>     ps[5,i,t,3] <- 0
>
>     ps[5,i,t,4] <- 0
>
>     ps[5,i,t,5] <- 1
>
>
>
>     # Define probabilities of O(t) given S(t)
>
>     po[1,i,t,1] <- 1
>
>     po[1,i,t,2] <- 0
>
>     po[1,i,t,3] <- 0
>
>     po[1,i,t,4] <- 0
>
>     po[2,i,t,1] <- 0
>
>     po[2,i,t,2] <- 0
>
>     po[2,i,t,3] <- 0
>
>     po[2,i,t,4] <- 1
>
>     po[3,i,t,1] <- 0
>
>     po[3,i,t,2] <- 1
>
>     po[3,i,t,3] <- 0
>
>     po[3,i,t,4] <- 0
>
>     po[4,i,t,1] <- 0
>
>     po[4,i,t,2] <- 0
>
>     po[4,i,t,3] <- 1
>
>     po[4,i,t,4] <- 0
>
>     po[5,i,t,1] <- 0
>
>     po[5,i,t,2] <- 0
>
>     po[5,i,t,3] <- 0
>
>     po[5,i,t,4] <- 1
>
>     } #t
>
>     } #i
>
>
>
>     # Likelihood
>
>     for (i in 1:nind){
>
>     # Define latent state at first capture   # all individuals are captured as alive and active radiotracker => 1
>
>     z[i,f[i]] <- 1
>
>     for (t in (f[i]+1):n.occasions){
>
>     # State process: draw S(t) given S(t-1)
>
>     z[i,t] ~ dcat(ps[z[i,t-1], i, t-1,])
>
>     # Observation process: draw O(t) given S(t)
>
>     y[i,t] ~ dcat(po[z[i,t], i, t-1,])
>
>     } #t
>
>     } #i
>
>     }
>
>     ",fill = TRUE)
>
> sink()
>
>
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi Tina, sometimes it is helpful to have additional comments in the code for the multistate probabilities to keep things obvious.  For example:

#po[true,i,t,obs]

This indicates the location of the true latent state index vs. the observed state index.  I think you have a couple errors in the observed states:

po[3,i,t,1] <- pNB[t]
po[3,i,t,2] <- 0
po[3,i,t,3] <- 0
po[3,i,t,4] <- 1-pNB[t]

This is saying that the probability of observing state 1 (seen as breeder) when the true state is 3 (non-breeder) is pNB[t].  That probability should be zero, no?  You should never be observing a nonbreeder as a breeder, unless there is state miss-classification error.  I think pNB[t] should be located at po[3,i,t,2].  The same goes for the pJ[t] probability, which should be at po[4,i,t,3].
